| [NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse with delay alone, so a person is a population of interests that forestall one another. | [NOTE-953](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-953.md) | Sung, Rigotti & Lee — factorized goal and uncertainty codes in lateral PFC | A reanalysis of 20 people's fMRI from a 2014 two-stage Markov task with cued goals and block-wise transition noise. | [NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md) | Flayelle et al. — A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | A narrative review and a taxonomy. Design features of six kinds of online service are linked, mostly by cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect evidence, to loss of control. They are sorted by the learning and control process each exploits. Model-free: reinforcement schedules and personalized triggers. Model-based: overvaluation, interference with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases. Providers select features by their effect on use and revenue, and personalize them under informational asymmetry. For the record it maps closely onto the parts of the potential account: features that strengthen a cue-keyed ranking, move its reference course, falsify the user's reading of progress, or pre-empt the other perspectives. | Read |
| [NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md) | Berridge and Robinson — Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction | An invited review of the incentive-sensitization theory by its authors. 'Wanting' and 'liking' have dissociable brain systems. Drugs can sensitize the 'wanting' system so that it is lastingly hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts while 'liking' stays flat or falls. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose cognitive desire, run without report, and grow in abstinence, and the theory is being extended, on weak evidence, to behavioural addictions. For the record it is a mechanism for proxy-keyed potential in persons. | [NOTE-1117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1117.md) | The power of goal-directed processes in the causation of emotional and other actions | A reversal of the default in dual-process models of action and emotion. Goal-directed processes, which select the action option with the highest expected utility, can be fast and automatic, so they, not stimulus-driven habits or appraisal-to-action-tendency links, are the default cause of action. Most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, and values and expectancies settle it. Emotional actions are those whose tendencies have control precedence because the goals at stake are highly valued, so emotional episodes are decision processes with higher stakes. | Read |
| [NOTE-1120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1120.md) | Brown, Price & Dombrovski — Anxiety as a disorder of uncertainty | A narrative review and theoretical proposal, with no new data and no simulation. Computational learning studies of anxiety (seven, not a systematic search) find altered adjustment of learning rate to kinds of uncertainty, mostly with aversive outcomes, rather than inflated threat learning or valuation. The authors propose that in aversive environments avoidance of uncertain states keeps their uncertainty high and so perpetuates itself, that anxiety amplifies this by misreading noise as change, and that exposure works by reducing the uncertainty, not the threat. It covers fear-based disorders and says it does not explain GAD. | Read |
| [NOTE-1123](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1123.md) | De Kleine et al. — Impaired action-safety learning and excessive relief during avoidance | A cross-sectional comparison of 47 healthy controls with 139 treatment-seeking patients (33 OCD, 40 panic disorder with agoraphobia, 66 PTSD) in a picture-based avoidance task. | [NOTE-1127](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1127.md) | Chou, Wilson & Smith — The influence of anxiety on exploration | A narrative review of computational modelling studies of anxiety and exploration, almost all in reward tasks and sub-clinical samples. | [NOTE-1130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1130.md) | Gerstner et al. — Eligibility traces and plasticity on behavioral time scales | A review by theoreticians. In a three-factor rule, pre- and postsynaptic co-activation sets a decaying synaptic flag, the eligibility trace, and the weight changes only if a third signal (reward minus expected reward, surprise, novelty, or a neuron-specific error) arrives while it is set. Five experimental papers (2014–2017), mostly in slices, give traces of about 1 s in striatum, 3–10 s in cortex, about 2 s and about a minute in hippocampus. The authors grant that other mechanisms could bridge the same gap. | Read |
| [NOTE-1134](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1134.md) | Mancinelli & Bach — A systematic review of human avoidance learning | A PRISMA systematic review, not a meta-analysis, of 116 studies of avoidance learning in healthy humans with shock or noise (1939–2024). Avoidance is learned without terminating the CS, transfers by inference to stimuli never paired with harm, and persists when it can be performed, longest when it is most effective; this contradicts two-factor theory and favours expectancy and inference. But some avoidance persists after the US is visibly removed, which a purely inferential account does not predict. No clinical samples were included. | Read |
| [NOTE-1136](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1136.md) | Zorowitz, Momennejad & Daw — Anxiety, avoidance, and sequential evaluation | A decision-theoretic argument with simulations, no data. In sequential evaluation the ability to avoid danger later should make it less threatening now. An agent that computes values as if it will fail to avoid later (a β-pessimistic Bellman equation, weight w) spreads negative value to states far from the threat and avoids early, which reproduces qualitatively exaggerated threat appraisal, generalization, earlier cash-out in risk tasks and aversive pruning, and predicts a reduced free-choice premium. The misbelief concerns the agent's own future control, not the danger. | Read |
| [NOTE-1137](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1137.md) | Craske et al. — Maximizing exposure therapy: an inhibitory learning approach | A clinical translation, not a study. It summarizes evidence that extinction leaves the original threat association intact and adds a competing inhibitory one, so fear can return. It argues that exposure should aim to violate expectancies, not to reduce fear within a session, and that fear reduction during exposure does not predict outcome. It sets out strategies for strengthening and retrieving inhibitory learning, with five invented case examples. | [NOTE-1138](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1138.md) | Friston et al. — Active inference and learning | A discrete-state active inference scheme in which a habit is one more policy, a state-to-state transition model learned by counting observed transitions, and the prior over policies is learned by counting which policies were pursued. | [NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md) | Börgers & Sarin — Learning through reinforcement and replicator dynamics | A short theoretical paper. One Bush–Mosteller learner with payoffs in (0, 1), Cross's model, moves in expectation as a population under the discrete replicator step, and in the continuous-time limit follows the Taylor replicator dynamic at any finite time. For every learning speed, though, the discrete process is absorbed in a pure strategy profile with probability one. With negative payoffs a probability-matching force enters beside a replicator force. Proofs are by Euler's method and Norman's theorems on slow learning; the negative-payoff limit is stated with its proof omitted. | Read |
